title: Cap. VII: Infant death and Adam's sin — two senses; only mediate imputation conceded
pass_a_gloss: Yet from there Garissoles draws this argument: to those on whom the penalty of death is laid for sin, sin is imputed. But before the law the penalty of death for Adam's sin was laid on infants. Therefore Adam's sin was imputed to them. Placeus answers: Adam's sin is taken in two ways. (1) As the sin propagated from him into posterity and multiplied by the number of men — called flesh and the old Adam. (2) As the cause of that propagated sin, namely Adam's actual disobedience. If the first way, he grants the whole argument: that sin, because it is inside us, is rightly imputed to us all, even infants. If the second way, he distinguishes the preposition 'on account of' (propter): it can mean the near or immediate cause, or only the remote or mediate one. If the near sense, he denies the minor: infants' death-penalty is laid immediately for the inherent vice, remotely for Adam's actual sin. If the remote sense, only mediate imputation of that actual sin follows — which he freely grants. Calvin taught him this: because Adam's sin is the cause of our sin, Paul ascribes our ruin to him; by 'our sin' Calvin means what is inborn and what we are born with. Bullinger: Adam's fall would not hurt us unless such perversity or corruption were inborn in us from it as would deserve God's judgment.
pass_b_english: Yet from there he draws out this argument: "To those on whom the penalty of death is inflicted on account of sin, sin is imputed. But before the law the penalty of death on account of Adam's sin was inflicted on infants. Therefore Adam's sin was imputed to them." I answer: Adam's sin is taken in two ways: (1) for that sin which, propagated from him into posterity and multiplied according to the number of men, is called flesh and the old Adam; (2) for the cause of that propagated sin, namely Adam's actual disobedience. If it is taken in the former way, I grant the whole argument. For I confess that that sin, because it is within us, is rightly imputed to us all, even to infants. If in the latter way, I distinguish the preposition "on account of": for it signifies either the near or immediate cause, or only the remote or mediate. If the former, I deny the minor proposition: the penalty of death was inflicted on infants immediately on account of the inherent vice, remotely on account of Adam's actual sin. If the latter, there follows only a mediate imputation of that actual sin, which I freely grant. Calvin taught me this, because, he says, Adam's sin is the cause of our sin, and Paul ascribes our ruin to him (Romans 5). "I call our sin," he says, "that which is inborn in us, and with which we are born." And Bullinger: "Adam's fall would not hurt us unless such perversity or corruption had been inborn in us from it as would deserve God's judgment" (Decades).
source_text: Sed tamen inde hoc argumentum elicit. Quibus irrogatur poena mortis propter peccatum, iis peccatum imputatur. Atqui infantibus irrogata est ante legem poena mortis propter peccatum Adae. Ergo iis peccatum Adae imputatum est. Resp. Peccatum Adae duobus modis accipi: 1. pro eo peccato, quod ab eo in posteros propagatum & secundum hominum numerum multiplicatum, caro & vetus Adam appellatur. 2. pro causa peccati illius propagati, nempe actuali Adae inobedientia. Si priore modo accipitur, concedo totum argumentum. Fateor enim peccatum illud, quia intra nos est, nobis omnibus, etiam infantibus, merito imputari. Si posteriore modo, distinguo praepositionem propter: nam vel causam proximam seu immediatam, vel remotam tantum seu mediatam significat. Si prius, nego minorem propositionem: irrogata est infantibus poena mortis proxime ob inhaerens vitium, remote ob Adami actuale peccatum. Si posterius, inde sequitur duntaxat peccati illius actualis imputatio mediata, quam ultro concedo. Hoc me docuit Calvinus, quia, inquit, ejus peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum illi Paulus ascribit. Peccatum nostrum voco, quod nobis ingenitum est, & cum quo nascimur. Et Bullingerus, non noceret nobis Adae lapsus, nisi talis ex eo perversitas seu corruptio nobis innata fuisset, quae Dei judicium promeretur.
